title: Show like a pro

slides.title: Show like a pro
slides.body:
Prepare the tour.
Listen after the showing.
Agree on the next step.

Today’s practiceAsk about the showing and agree on what happens next.Work with a partner. Give specific feedback. Try again.
slides.notes: Invite a recent example from one person, then begin. Keep the opening to two minutes.
slides.cue: Ask: What would you like to get better at today?

slides.title: What makes a showing uncomfortable?
slides.body: “I barely had a chance to look. The agent kept telling me what I should like.”
slides.notes: Take three short answers. Ask agents to describe behavior rather than personality. Connect those answers to space, useful questions, and an agreed next step.
slides.cue: What could you stop doing on your next showing?

slides.title: Confirm access and the required agreement
slides.lead: Know what needs to be signed before touring.
slides.body:
Before the appointment

Confirm access, showing instructions, and the brokerage’s current agreement requirements.

With the buyer

Zillow’s touring agreement covers touring for seven days without compensation or exclusivity. Explain the actual approved form and allow questions.

Before entering

Confirm the required agreement is complete. If something is missing, resolve it before touring.
slides.notes: Use the form and instructions approved by your brokerage. Zillow’s current product page confirms its seven-day touring agreement. That term describes this product, not every buyer agreement. Confirm the current product and local requirements before teaching the form. This is a process check, not legal advice.
slides.cue: How would you explain the agreement before the appointment?

slides.title: Give the buyer useful comparisons
slides.body:
Plan the route

When appropriate, prepare two or three homes that help compare the buyer’s stated priorities.

Bring context

Review available property information, comparable homes, and relevant buyer materials.

Confirm the details

Check access and current status for each home. Explain any changes promptly.
slides.notes: Use actual availability when preparing a real tour. Avoid adding homes just to make the tour longer. Ask agents to explain one useful comparison.
slides.cue: What would make a second home worth including?

slides.title: Let the buyer look first
slides.lead: Stay available without following them through every room.
slides.body:
Give them space

Let them explore at their own pace while following property and safety instructions.

Stay easy to find

A suitable entry or kitchen area may work. Explain where you will be.

Answer useful questions

Share verified information. Say what you need to check. Avoid narrating every feature.
slides.notes: Ask someone to demonstrate an opening at the door. Respect seller instructions and actual safety needs. Availability matters more than standing in one prescribed place.
slides.cue: What will you say before the buyer starts looking?

slides.title: Let the buyer have their own preferences
slides.lead: Your taste may be different from theirs.
slides.body: The buyer likes a feature you dislike. What helps?
slides.notes: Use a fictional vaulted-ceiling example from the source material. Distinguish personal taste from material or safety concerns that must be addressed accurately.
slides.cue: When does an observation need to be raised even if it is not your preference?

slides.title: Ask permission to compare impressions
slides.lead: Find out whether any home is worth pursuing.
slides.body:
“Before we head out, can we compare what you thought? Did any of these feel like a home you would want to make an offer on?”

If the answer is no

Thank them for being direct. Learn what was missing.

If the answer is yes

Find out which home and why. Then discuss what is needed to act.
slides.notes: Have the buyer role say no first. The agent should accept it comfortably and ask a useful follow-up. A negative answer is useful information.
slides.cue: What would you ask after “None of them felt right”?

slides.title: Use a rating to start a conversation
slides.lead: The reason matters more than the number.
slides.body:
“On a scale of one to ten, how close was that home to what you want?”

“What makes it an eight?”

“What was missing?”
slides.notes: Ask partners to give the same rating for different reasons. Show why the number alone is not enough for a note or a search decision.
slides.cue: How would two buyers’ eights mean different things?

slides.title: Ask about financing in context
slides.lead: Once you have discussed the home, learn what preparation is needed.
slides.body:
“If we found the right home, would you be buying with cash or working with a lender?”

Already has a lender

Ask what has been reviewed and whether the buyer has questions. Respect that relationship.

Needs help

Offer an introduction with permission. The lender handles detailed financial information.
slides.notes: This is a conversation after the showing, distinct from the first-call LEAD sequence. Do not collect private income or credit details in a sidewalk conversation.
slides.cue: What would you ask if they say their bank has already helped?

slides.title: Ask what is behind the timing
slides.lead: A date is more useful when you understand why it matters.
slides.body: “You mentioned six months. Is there a date you need to work around, or is that more of a preference?”
slides.notes: Ask permission before exploring a sensitive reason. Do not assume a round number is a firm deadline. If they mention a lease, ask about the actual date and flexibility.
slides.cue: What changes if the lease ends on a fixed date?

slides.title: Match the plan to this buyer
slides.lead: Agree on what is useful now.
slides.body:
Wants to offer soon

Discuss the home, required preparation, financing questions, and the next call.

Moving in several months

Work backward from the real deadline. Confirm the next decision and when to revisit it.

Timing is still uncertain

Agree on useful information and a follow-up. Do not force a lender call the buyer does not need.
slides.notes: Ask agents to explain why the same next step would not fit all three buyers. Use actual market, lender, and transaction timelines; do not teach a fixed number of days as universal.
slides.cue: Which next step would be premature for this buyer?

slides.title: Work backward from a real deadline
slides.lead: Confirm the steps with the people responsible for them.
slides.body:
Start at the deadline

When does the buyer need access to the next home? What flexibility exists?

Check the process

Confirm likely transaction timing, financing work, and available inventory.

Agree on the next appointment

Name its purpose, date, and time. Confirm what each person will do before it.
slides.notes: Use a fictional lease-end example. Avoid presenting an estimated closing date as a guarantee. Have the buyer repeat the plan to catch different expectations.
slides.cue: What needs confirmation before you promise a date?

slides.title: Practice the first question after a showing
slides.lead: Let the buyer answer before asking the next question.
slides.body:
First attempt

Ask whether any home is worth pursuing.

Buyer response

Say no, or give a rating with a reason.

Feedback and retry

Did the agent accept the answer and ask a relevant follow-up? Retry one part.
slides.notes: Pairs take 60 seconds each with 30 seconds feedback and a short retry. Do not stack all five questions into one long sentence.
slides.cue: Did the buyer have enough time to answer?

slides.title: Practice a conversation about timing
slides.lead: Ask what makes the date important.
slides.body:
“I guess six months.”

“My lease ends November 30.”

“I would move sooner for the right place.”
slides.notes: Give each partner a different response. Ask the agent to learn whether the date is fixed, flexible, or still uncertain. Do not pressure the buyer to move earlier.
slides.cue: What did you learn that changes the plan?

slides.title: Run the conversation after a showing
slides.lead: Agent, buyer, observer. Rotate after each round.
slides.notes: Three rounds: 3-minute conversation, 1-minute feedback, 1-minute retry. Rotate all roles. Judge the usefulness of the questions and plan, not whether the agent recites every example word for word.
slides.cue: Observer: what did the agent learn that would change the next step?

slides.title: Record what the showing changed
slides.lead: Use the stage definitions from Day 1.
slides.body:
Stage

Met with customer after the first appointment. Showing homes after the second appointment. Move further only when the event happens.

Note

Which homes, what the buyer liked, what was missing, and the reason for their timing.

Task

The agreed next action with a date and time.
slides.notes: Correct the source deck’s blanket instruction to use Showing homes after every showing. Ask an agent to explain the stage based on the actual event.
slides.cue: Would another agent know why you chose the next homes?

slides.title: Write the follow-up record
slides.lead: Use the practice buyer you just worked with.
slides.body:
Check your work
Stage matches the event. Note includes specific preferences and timing without guesses. Task names the agreed action and date. Ask your coach to review the record.
slides.notes: This is a coach-reviewed written exercise, not an automated grade. Partners compare against the criteria and revise one missing detail.
slides.cue: Which detail could someone act on tomorrow?

slides.title: What would you ask without the slides?
slides.lead: Recall the questions before checking the guide.
slides.body:
Compare with the lesson
Is any home worth pursuing? How close is it to what you want? What explains that rating? How will you prepare to purchase? What is behind your timing? Then summarize and agree on the next step.
slides.notes: Give 45 seconds without notes. Accept natural wording and a conversation that follows the buyer. Correct an omitted topic through a short spoken retry.
slides.cue: Which answer most often changes your plan?

slides.title: Before your next client conversation
slides.lead: Write down when you will practice again.
slides.body:
At your next showing

Give the buyer space, then ask about the experience.

After the conversation

Save preferences, timing, and the agreed task in Follow Up Boss.

Before Day 4

Bring one question buyers ask when financing comes up.
slides.notes: Ask each agent to name one behavior they will practice. Within 24 hours, ask them to explain it without notes. In three days, use a new scenario. In seven days, review an actual example. These are suggested coaching intervals; no reminders are sent.
slides.cue: Tell your partner what you will practice and when.

cases.name: Jordan · ready to offer
cases.quote: “The second house is a nine. I would like to offer, but I have not sent my lender the documents.”
cases.goal: Learn why it is a nine. Clarify preparation and agree on a useful next step.

cases.name: Morgan · fixed deadline
cases.quote: “The layout was good, but neither had the outdoor space I need. My lease ends November 30.”
cases.goal: Learn the missing criteria and whether the date has flexibility. Agree on the next search and appointment.

cases.name: Alex · flexible timing
cases.quote: “Nothing felt quite right. I said six months, but I am not working toward a deadline.”
cases.goal: Accept the answer. Learn what was missing and agree on a follow-up the buyer finds useful.
